desc:
Take all substrings of s that have length exactly k, one for every start position. Count the pairs of start positions (i, j) with i < j whose two substrings are anagrams of each other (same letters with the same multiplicities, any order). Equal substrings are anagrams of each other too.

s = "abbaab", k = 2
windows: ab bb ba aa ab
anagram groups: {ab, ba, ab} (3 windows), {bb}, {aa}
pairs: 3
result = 3
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing every pair of windows is O(n<sup>2</sup>) comparisons, too slow for 8,000 windows.
Two windows are anagrams exactly when their letter-count vectors are equal. Group windows by that vector.

Maintain the 26 counters while sliding, use a snapshot of them (for example a tuple) as a hash key, and for a group of size g add g * (g - 1) / 2 pairs. Equivalently, add the current group size before incrementing it.
editorial: Let a window's signature be its vector of 26 letter counts. Two windows are anagrams if and only if their signatures are equal, so the task becomes: count pairs of equal keys. Update the counters in O(1) when sliding the window (one letter in, one letter out), then convert the counters to a tuple key in O(26).

Keep a dictionary from signature to how many windows had it so far. When a new window arrives, all earlier windows with the same signature form a new pair with it, so add the dictionary value to the answer and then increment it. This yields the number of pairs in total. Time O(26 · n), space O(26 · n). The answer is at most n(n-1)/2, which is below 32 million here.
